excerpt: A letter of protection lets you get medical treatment now and pay from your settlement later. How they work in Georgia and South Carolina.
keyTakeaways: A letter of protection (LOP) is a written agreement, signed by you and your attorney, promising a medical provider that its bills will be paid out of your settlement or verdict, so you can get treatment without paying up front. You remain responsible for the bill. LOPs are common in Georgia and South Carolina personal injury cases where victims lack health insurance or face coverage gaps. Georgia gives hospitals, physician practices and other providers a statutory lien on your injury claim (O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470); South Carolina has no hospital-lien statute, so South Carolina providers rely on contract — often a letter of protection. Insurance companies may attack LOPs by arguing provider bias. In Georgia, for injuries on or after April 21, 2025, the insurer can obtain the letter itself, itemized charges, any sale of the bill to a third party and its price, and who referred you (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1(d)). Attorneys can often negotiate LOP balances down after settlement.

faqs.question: What is a letter of protection in a personal injury case?
faqs.answer: A letter of protection (LOP) is a written agreement between your attorney and a medical provider guaranteeing that the provider will be paid from the proceeds of your personal injury settlement or verdict. The LOP allows you to receive medical treatment without paying out of pocket while your case is pending. You remain responsible for the bill.

faqs.question: Is a letter of protection legally binding?
faqs.answer: Yes. An LOP is a contractual agreement that obligates you to pay the medical provider from your settlement proceeds. If your case is unsuccessful and you recover nothing, you may still owe the medical bills. It also binds your attorney: once settlement money comes in, ethics rules in both states require the attorney to protect the provider's claim to it rather than pay it all out to you.

faqs.question: Do all doctors accept letters of protection?
faqs.answer: No. Many doctors and medical facilities are selective about which LOPs they accept. Providers are more likely to accept an LOP from an attorney they have an established professional relationship with and trust to resolve the case. In Georgia, for injuries on or after April 21, 2025, the insurer can learn who referred you to an LOP provider (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1(d)(4)).

faqs.question: How do insurance companies use letters of protection against me?
faqs.answer: Insurance companies may argue that doctors treating you under an LOP have a financial incentive to exaggerate your injuries or recommend unnecessary treatment. Your attorney can counter this by presenting objective medical evidence and pointing out that the doctor's professional reputation depends on honest assessments. In Georgia cases arising on or after April 21, 2025, the insurer can obtain the LOP itself, itemized billing, any sale of the bill to a factoring company and the price paid, and who referred you — and both sides may challenge the reasonableness and necessity of the treatment (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1(d), (f)).

faqs.question: Can my attorney negotiate the medical bills under an LOP?
faqs.answer: Yes. Attorneys routinely negotiate reductions on LOP balances, which directly increases your take-home settlement amount.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an LOP and a medical lien?
faqs.answer: An LOP is a voluntary agreement arranged by your attorney, usually before or early in treatment. A medical lien is a statutory right that hospitals and providers can assert after treatment. In Georgia, hospitals, physician practices and certain other providers have a statutory lien under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470. South Carolina has no hospital-lien statute; providers there rely on contract, including letters of protection.
